Methodology: the pipeline as an estimator

Source: vignettes/methodology.qmd 
library(catchmentACS)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)

# Force network-free, deterministic builds: no provider/Census calls, no cache.
old_options <- options(
  catchmentACS.progress = "off",
  catchmentACS.rate_first_default = FALSE
)
old_cache <- getOption("catchmentACS.cache_enabled", NULL)
on.exit(options(old_options), add = TRUE)
on.exit(options(catchmentACS.cache_enabled = old_cache), add = TRUE)
cacs_set_cache(FALSE, scope = "session")

This article is the entry point to the package’s method track. It frames the whole catchmentACS pipeline as a single statistical estimator, fixes the notation that the deeper theory articles reuse, names the six estimand families the package is built around, and shows — in real numbers, on the bundled fixtures — why a count and an average are aggregated with different weights. Where the applied articles answer “how do I run this?”, this one answers “what, exactly, is being estimated, and by what formula?”

It is deliberately math-light and does not re-derive the math: each estimand family and each margin-of-error (MOE) formula has a full derivation in a dedicated theory article, and this overview states the result and points there. The three companion articles are vignette("theory-spatial-aggregation", package = "catchmentACS"), vignette("theory-moe-propagation", package = "catchmentACS"), and vignette("theory-derived-rates", package = "catchmentACS"). By the end you should be able to read any catchment estimate as \text{estimate} \pm \text{MOE} and know which of six families produced it.

If you want to run the pipeline rather than read its math, start with vignette("getting-started", package = "catchmentACS") and vignette("alabama-tutorial", package = "catchmentACS").

About the data in this article

Every executable cell here is built entirely from the package’s bundled inst/extdata fixtures — the synthetic legacy_2025_* objects and the sample_alabama_subset ACS extract — so this article renders with no Census, OSRM, ORS, or other network calls. These fixtures preserve the production calling contract (sites, drive-time polygons, tract-level ACS variables) but are synthetic and illustrative: they are included only for examples, tests, and reproducible package checks. They are not live Alabama policy estimates and must not be cited as real ACS results. Any real analysis requires a fresh live run (see vignette("providers", package = "catchmentACS")).

The pipeline is an estimator

It helps to read the whole pipeline as one estimator. cacs_run() looks like a data-processing wrapper, but statistically it is one estimator with five stages. Two stages reach data sources; the last three are deterministic computation on whatever those returned:

cacs_acs_prefetch() (ACS download) → cacs_isochrone() (routing) → cacs_intersect_weight() → cacs_propagate_moe() → cacs_derive_rates().

The estimand is a neighborhood characteristic inside a drive-time catchment. The ACS publishes its estimates on census tracts, which do not line up with catchments — a drive-time area slices through tract boundaries. So the estimator re-expresses tract-level published values as catchment-level values by area-weighted aggregation, then carries the published uncertainty through that aggregation. Concretely, for each site s:

  1. Sites → catchments. Take the drive-time isochrone polygon I_s (drawn fresh, or reused from precomputed polygons) and the ACS tract polygons T_j.
  2. Catchments → tract overlaps. Cut the intersections I_s \cap T_j on an equal-area projection, and from each intersection build a weight describing how much of tract j the catchment captures.
  3. Overlaps → estimates. Aggregate each tract-level estimate Y_j (or X_j) to the catchment with the weight that matches the variable’s estimand family.
  4. Estimates → margins of error. Propagate the published tract-level MOEs through the same weights.
  5. Estimates → rates. Form the curated derived rates as ratios of aggregated numerators and denominators, each with its own propagated MOE.

The single function cacs_run() chains these stages; the five pipeline functions expose each one on its own. Two choices in steps 2–3 carry the entire statistical content of the package, and they are the reason the rest of this article exists: which weight, and which family. Get either wrong and the arithmetic still runs — it just estimates the wrong thing, silently.

Shared notation

The whole method track uses the same symbols. Establishing them once here lets the three theory articles stay terse.

Symbol Meaning
I_s the drive-time isochrone (catchment) polygon for site s (a cumulative ring)
T_j census tract j
I_s \cap T_j the part of tract j that falls inside the catchment
\lvert\,\cdot\,\rvert equal-area measure (area on EPSG:5070, in \text{m}^2)
Y_j a tract-level count ACS estimate (extensive: persons, households)
X_j a tract-level scalar / proxy ACS estimate (intensive: a median, a per-capita figure)
A_j, B_j a ratio’s numerator and denominator counts in tract j
M_j the published 90% margin of error for the tract-level estimate

Two weights do all the work. The coverage weight is the fraction of a tract’s area captured by the catchment,

w^{cov}_{sj} = \frac{\lvert I_s \cap T_j \rvert}{\lvert T_j \rvert},

and the normalized mean weight is the catchment’s intersection area for tract j as a share of all its intersection area,

w^{mean}_{sj} = \frac{\lvert I_s \cap T_j \rvert}{\sum_k \lvert I_s \cap T_k \rvert}, \qquad \sum_j w^{mean}_{sj} = 1,

so the mean weights sum to one within a site and drive-time cell. From these, the three estimator forms are

\widehat{Y}_s = \sum_j w^{cov}_{sj}\, Y_j, \qquad \widehat{\bar X}_s = \sum_j w^{mean}_{sj}\, X_j, \qquad \widehat{R}_s = \frac{\sum_j w^{cov}_{sj}\, A_j}{\sum_j w^{cov}_{sj}\, B_j}.

A spatial total allocates counts into the catchment with the coverage weight; a scalar/proxy mean blends intensive values with the normalized mean weight; a derived rate aggregates the numerator and denominator each as a coverage total, then divides. Throughout, standard errors and margins of error are interconvertible through the Census multiplier at the 90% level,

M = 1.645\, SE, \qquad SE = \frac{M}{1.645},

and every margin of error in the pipeline is reported at that level: variances accumulate on the SE scale and convert back at the end.

The six estimand families at a glance

A variable’s estimand family decides which weight aggregates it and which MOE path applies. This is the central methodological point of the package, and the spatial aggregation algorithm is built around it: a count and a median are aggregated by different weights, and using the wrong one is a silent statistical error, not a runtime failure.

Estimand family Example variable Point estimate Weight
spatial_total total population; persons in poverty (B17001_002) \widehat{Y}_s = \sum_j w^{cov}_{sj} Y_j coverage w^{cov}_{sj}
derived_rate poverty rate; SNAP rate \widehat{R}_s = \dfrac{\sum_j w^{cov}_{sj} A_j}{\sum_j w^{cov}_{sj} B_j} coverage (numerator and denominator separately)
area_weighted_scalar_proxy per-capita income (B19301_001) \widehat{\bar X}_s = \sum_j w^{mean}_{sj} X_j normalized mean w^{mean}_{sj}
population_weighted_scalar_proxy (reserved) scalar proxy under population weighting \widehat{\bar X}_s = \sum_j w^{mean}_{sj} X_j population-normalized mean
median_proxy tract median household income (B19013_001) weighted blend of tract medians, not the true catchment median normalized mean w^{mean}_{sj}
metadata_only provenance fields no numeric aggregation none

Read the table by weight. An extensive count like persons in poverty must be summed into the catchment with the coverage weight — half a tract contributes half its people. An intensive scalar like per-capita income must be averaged with the normalized mean weight — half a tract does not contribute “half a dollar per person,” so the contributions average rather than accumulate. Derived rates are a special case: numerator and denominator are each aggregated as coverage-weighted totals, then divided, so the rate inherits the coverage path. The median_proxy family is labelled a proxy on purpose — a weighted blend of tract medians is not the true median of the pooled catchment population, and the package keeps that caveat attached to the estimate.

Add an intensive variable as if it were a count, or divide a count by a weight sum as if it were an average, and you get a number with no defensible interpretation. Nothing errors; the result is just wrong. The family classifier is what stops that from happening — and the next section shows the two paths diverging on actual fixture numbers.

Two families are scaffolding rather than active estimators in this release. In weight_method = "area" (the implemented path), the area forms of the weights above are active. population_weighted_scalar_proxy and the population mean weight are a reserved future surface; weight_method = "population" fails loud at the orchestrator boundary today. metadata_only rows carry provenance and receive no numeric aggregation. The classifier and the per-family aggregation are documented in the “Estimand families and weights” section of ?cacs_intersect_weight.

A worked example: coverage total vs mean proxy

This is the section to read slowly. We take one site and one ring from the fixtures, look at the weights the package builds, and then watch a count and an average go through their two different aggregation paths — so the abstract w^{cov}-vs-w^{mean} distinction lands as real numbers. The same contract scales to many sites and drive times.

We use the synthetic site AL_SITE_03 at a 15-minute drive time, whose catchment intersects three tracts. First, intersect and keep the per-tract audit so we can see the geometry ingredients:

# These fixtures are exactly the shapes stages 1-2 would have returned, frozen.
sites <- readRDS(system.file(
  "extdata", "legacy_2025_sites.rds", package = "catchmentACS"
))
iso <- readRDS(system.file(
  "extdata", "legacy_2025_isochrones.rds", package = "catchmentACS"
))
acs <- readRDS(system.file(
  "extdata", "sample_alabama_subset.rds", package = "catchmentACS"
))

site_id    <- "AL_SITE_03"
drive_time <- 15L

iso_one <- iso[
  iso$site_id == site_id & iso$drive_time_min == drive_time, ,
  drop = FALSE
]

weighted <- cacs_intersect_weight(
  iso_sf           = iso_one,
  acs_sf           = acs,
  weight_method    = "area",
  keep_tract_audit = TRUE,
  verbose          = FALSE
)

The tract audit holds, for each tract the catchment touched, the intersection area and the tract area. From those two columns the package forms both weights. Computing them side by side makes the difference concrete:

audit <- attr(weighted, "cacs_tract_audit") |>
  transmute(
    GEOID,
    int_area_m2,
    tract_area_m2,
    w_cov  = int_area_m2 / tract_area_m2,            # coverage weight
    w_mean = int_area_m2 / sum(int_area_m2)          # normalized mean weight
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(int_area_m2))

audit
# A tibble: 3 × 5
  GEOID       int_area_m2 tract_area_m2 w_cov w_mean
  <chr>             <dbl>         <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
1 01001000201    9543830.      9543830.  1.00  0.333
2 01133000101    9543830.      9543830.  1.00  0.333
3 01003000201    9543830.      9543830.  1.00  0.333
c(
  sum_w_cov  = sum(audit$w_cov),    # NOT constrained to 1
  sum_w_mean = sum(audit$w_mean)    # constrained to 1 by construction
)
 sum_w_cov sum_w_mean
         3          1

Read the two sums. The coverage weights w^{cov}_{sj} each measure how much of that tract the catchment captured, so they do not sum to one — here they sum to the effective number of tract-equivalents the catchment covers. The mean weights w^{mean}_{sj} are renormalized to sum to exactly one. That single structural difference is what separates a total from an average.

Now send a count through the coverage path. Persons in poverty (B17001_002) is a spatial_total, so the package reports \widehat{Y}_s = \sum_j w^{cov}_{sj}\,Y_j with weight_basis = "coverage":

weighted |>
  filter(variable == "B17001_002") |>
  select(variable, estimate, moe, weight_sum, n_tracts,
         estimand_family, weight_basis)
# A tibble: 1 × 7
  variable   estimate   moe weight_sum n_tracts estimand_family weight_basis
  <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>    <int> <chr>           <chr>
1 B17001_002     2165  179.          3        3 spatial_total   coverage

The weight_sum column is exactly \sum_j w^{cov}_{sj} — the same not-equal-to-one sum from the audit — and estimate is the coverage-weighted count of people in poverty across the three partial tracts. That is a total: it scales with how much area the catchment captures.

Now send an average through. Per-capita income (B19301_001) is an area_weighted_scalar_proxy: an intensive, per-person quantity that must be blended, not summed. Its estimator is the normalized-mean-weighted average \widehat{\bar X}_s = \sum_j w^{mean}_{sj}\,X_j, whose weights sum to one within a site and drive-time cell, so the result stays on the per-person scale and lies between the contributing tracts’ own values. (For the implementation see ?cacs_intersect_weight; for the full derivation see vignette("theory-spatial-aggregation", package = "catchmentACS").)

The teaching moment is what happens if you ignore the family and aggregate this intensive variable as if it were a count. Below we pull the three tracts’ published per-capita incomes and apply both weights by hand, so the contrast is self-contained and exact:

pc_income <- acs |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(GEOID %in% audit$GEOID, variable == "B19301_001") |>
  select(GEOID, X = estimate)

demo <- audit |>
  select(GEOID, w_cov, w_mean) |>
  left_join(pc_income, by = "GEOID")

demo
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  GEOID       w_cov w_mean     X
  <chr>       <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 01001000201  1.00  0.333 22934
2 01133000101  1.00  0.333 20006
3 01003000201  1.00  0.333 37229
c(
  coverage_weighted_SUM = sum(demo$w_cov  * demo$X),   # wrong estimand for an average
  mean_weighted_PROXY   = sum(demo$w_mean * demo$X)    # correct: stays on the $/person scale
)
coverage_weighted_SUM   mean_weighted_PROXY
                80169                 26723

The two numbers tell the whole story. The coverage-weighted sum is 80169 — a dollar amount inflated past any single tract’s value, because summing an intensive quantity is meaningless. It is not an income anyone earns. The mean-weighted proxy is 26723, which stays on the per-person scale, between the tracts’ own values, which is what a catchment “average per-capita income” should be. Both used identical geometry; only the family-appropriate weight differs. This is the silent estimand error the family classifier exists to prevent, and it is why catchmentACS refuses to apply one weight to everything.

The MOE column moved with the estimate in both family rows above. How it is computed is the subject of the next section, in brief.

Margins of error in brief

ACS estimates ship with a published 90% margin of error, and that uncertainty must travel through the aggregation. cacs_propagate_moe() attaches an MOE to every row by dispatching on the estimand family. There are four MOE formula families; this article only names them and states the conversion.

  • Family A — weighted sum (for spatial_total): the root-sum-square of the coverage-weighted component MOEs.
  • Family B — weighted mean (for the *_scalar_proxy and median_proxy families): the same root-sum-square form with the normalized mean weights, which sum to one and are treated as fixed.
  • Family C1 — proportion subset (for a derived_rate whose numerator A is a true subset of its denominator B): the cross term is subtracted.
  • Family C2 — general ratio, conservative (the package’s default for the curated derived rates): the cross term is added, so the variance is always non-negative.

All four sit on the same conversion, M = 1.645\, SE: each component MOE is divided by 1.645 to a variance, the variances are combined, and the result is multiplied back by 1.645.

The one branch worth flagging here is the C1 → C2 fallback, and that it is never silent. When a Family C1 (proportion_subset) calculation yields a negative subset variance, the row is recomputed with the Family C2 (general_ratio_conservative) formula so a value is still produced, and the override is recorded per row: moe_formula_effective becomes "general_ratio_conservative", moe_fallback is set to TRUE, and moe_fallback_reason records the cause. A single summary warning reports the counts at the end of a run.

We do not derive these formulas here — including why variances accumulate on the SE scale and why the conservative ratio is the default. The full Family A/B/C1/C2 algebra, the independence assumptions, and the numerical guards live in vignette("theory-moe-propagation", package = "catchmentACS") and ?cacs_propagate_moe.

Projection and the within-tract assumption

Two modeling choices underpin every number above.

Equal-area measurement on EPSG:5070. The coverage weight w^{cov}_{sj} = \lvert I_s \cap T_j \rvert / \lvert T_j \rvert is a ratio of two areas, so it is only meaningful if numerator and denominator are measured in the same equal-area metric. The package transforms validated inputs to EPSG:5070 (NAD83 / CONUS Albers Equal Area) once before measuring any area, so equal physical areas carry equal weight regardless of where in the catchment they fall. This is also why the current release is scoped to the contiguous United States plus DC, where Albers distortion is negligible.

Uniform-within-tract allocation. Area weighting assumes the ACS characteristic is spread uniformly over each tract: a catchment that covers 30% of a tract’s area is credited with 30% of its count. This is exact for area but only approximate for people, and it is the standard areal-interpolation assumption that a future weight_method = "population" mode is designed to relax.

Both are stated only briefly here; the equal-area rationale and the uniform-within-tract assumption are argued in full in vignette("theory-spatial-aggregation", package = "catchmentACS").

Where the details live

This article is the map; the derivations are in the three method-track articles and the function reference, each reusing the notation fixed above.

  • Spatial aggregation — the coverage vs mean weight derivation, the per-site intersection algorithm, the full six-family aggregation table, EPSG:5070, and the within-tract assumption: vignette("theory-spatial-aggregation", package = "catchmentACS") and ?cacs_intersect_weight.
  • MOE propagation — the four formula families (A weighted sum, B weighted mean, C1 proportion subset, C2 conservative general ratio), the SE ↔︎ MOE relation, the never-silent C1 → C2 fallback, and the numerical guards: vignette("theory-moe-propagation", package = "catchmentACS") and ?cacs_propagate_moe.
  • Derived rates — the five curated rates, their ACS numerator/denominator pairs, the baseline C1/C2 policy, and the carrier-lookup mechanics: vignette("theory-derived-rates", package = "catchmentACS") and ?cacs_derive_rates.

For the record, each of the five curated rates maps to a fixed ACS numerator and denominator. ssi_rate is B19056_002 / B19056_001 — households with Supplemental Security Income over the B19056 household universe — and under the package’s baseline policy poverty_rate and labor_force_participation are C1-eligible (proportion_subset), while snap_rate, ssi_rate, and unemp_rate route to C2 (general_ratio_conservative). The full catalogue and dispatch rationale are in vignette("theory-derived-rates", package = "catchmentACS").

For the applied, run-it path that produces reporting tables from these same fixtures, see vignette("getting-started", package = "catchmentACS"), vignette("alabama-tutorial", package = "catchmentACS"), and vignette("providers", package = "catchmentACS").

Limitations

The estimator’s scope is deliberately narrow in this release.

  • Area weighting only. weight_method = "area" is implemented; the population-weighted scalar-proxy family and weight_method = "population" are a reserved fail-loud future surface. The uniform-within-tract assumption is exact for area, approximate for population.
  • Median is a proxy. A median_proxy value is a weighted blend of tract medians, not the true median of the pooled catchment population; it is labelled as a proxy throughout.
  • Conservative ratio MOE by default. Derived-rate MOEs default to the Family C2 general-ratio form; the tighter C1 subset form is opt-in for the C1-eligible rates and falls back to C2 (never silently) when its variance goes negative.
  • A fixed rate catalogue. The five curated rates are locked; arbitrary user-supplied ratios are deferred to a future release.
  • CONUS + DC. EPSG:5070 is the authoritative equal-area default for the contiguous United States and DC; the data path is ACS 5-year tract data for one state at a time, and other regions await a future CRS policy.
  • Fixtures. The bundled fixtures are synthetic and regression-oriented — useful for examples and package checks, not a substitute for a fresh live run when producing final analysis.

The interpretive caution that frames all of the above: an isochrone’s polygon area is provider- and snapshot-sensitive, so for policy reporting the tract membership, the weighted estimates, their margins of error, and the recorded provenance are more informative audit surfaces than raw polygon area alone. And, as the callout at the top stresses, the fixtures used here are synthetic — the numbers above illustrate the method, not Alabama.
